summary.title: What Every C Programmer Should Know About Undefined Behavior #1/3
summary.one_liner: Learn how C's undefined behaviors (signed overflow, oversized shifts, NULL dereference, type-punning through pointer casts) let compilers produce faster code, and why that trades away safety.
keywords: why does clang optimize away my check
c is not a high level assembler
compiler optimizations enabled by undefined behavior
takeaways: Signed integer overflow is undefined in C, which lets compilers simplify expressions like X+1 > X and optimize <= loops; unsigned overflow wraps and is defined.
Clang and GCC both treat several standard-undefined behaviors as undefined by default, and -fwrapv makes signed overflow defined at a performance cost.
Oversized shifts, wild pointer and out-of-bounds accesses, and NULL dereferences are undefined because hardware and performance costs of defining them are high.
Type-based alias analysis lets Clang turn a float array store loop into memset, but pointer casts that violate type rules break this; -fno-strict-aliasing disables it.
This post is part 1 of 3; the series covers why undefined behavior is risky when performance is not the only goal, and how LLVM and Clang handle it.
summary.summary: Chris Lattner opens a three-part series by explaining that C's undefined behavior is a deliberate trade for performance, not just a bug source. He walks through concrete cases: uninitialized variables, signed integer overflow (with loop and expression optimizations), oversized shift amounts, wild and NULL pointer dereferences, and type-rule violations. For each he explains the optimization enabled or overhead avoided, and notes the cost of defining the behavior instead. The post uses small C examples, including Clang turning a float store loop into memset, and mentions -fwrapv and -fno-strict-aliasing as the relevant flags.
